Following this introduction, the team worked on a filler task together to strengthen their bond and create a climate for idea generation. Their task was to try to come up with possible things to do with a brick, with an emphasis on the idea being creative, but yet usable. An example of a creative and useful idea is: ‘hollow the brick and use it as a vase’. Leaders received strict instructions to always react positively to an idea suggested by a Follower, regardless of their evaluation of the quality of the idea. Dependent Variables: Measures of Voice and Voice Quality. After the Follower had read the instructions and had 5 minutes to read through his or her information, the Leader made contact through a computer chat-window using the following line: “Hello, this is not an easy assignment. I have tackled it as follows: I gave every attribute an evaluation (positive, neutral, negative). The experimenter is on his way with my notes. Based on this, I select candidate B: that one has most positive attributes, least neutral and least negative. The other two are comparable. So I choose B, you can look at my notes if you want to know why.” The Leader did not specifically request a response, or ask for suggestions or ideas. The Follower was now in the possession of an information sheet of the Leader, with all attributes marked with either a green + (positive), a red -- (negative) or a blue N (neutral). Furthermore, the Followers had colored markers available if (s)he wished to organize his/her thoughts in a similar manner. So the Followers had full opportunity to find out that B was actually the least optimal choice, that A was only optimal from his/her own perspective, and that the best option for the team would be C. We assessed voice behavior by giving the Follower two choices: ‘Ok, I am fine with B’ (no voice), or ‘I think there is another possibility, let’s talk’ (voice). Please note that, knowing that the Leader would decide upon the pay-off, opposing the Leaders’ opinion

8 directly by voicing, entailed social risk: voicing could mean that the Follower would lose salary. If the Follower chose the second option, the simulated Leader asked which would be the Followers preferred candidate. The Follower also got the possibility to explain why (s)he would choose differently, but this was not requested. Voice quality was consequently assessed by what Followers voiced. Candidate A was lower in quality because this merely reflected the Followers’ initial preference and a sub-optimal choice considering all information. Switching to candidate C was considered a high-quality suggestion because this candidate was objectively the best team choice. Our most important expectation was that because people high in WMC have the ability to focus their attention for long periods of time, they would be more able to overcome the tendency to go for their initial choice, incorporate more possibilities, oversee more information, be more persistent and therefore have higher chances to get to the best solution for the team. In other words: WMC was expected to be highest in the group that suggested candidate C to the Leader. Checks Confederates and Control variables. As mentioned earlier, confederates were either male or female. Participants (randomly) assigned to either of these Leaders showed no differences in control variables. Both Leaders were (equally) perceived as competent, intelligent, trustworthy, appreciative Leader figures who took charge of the task. Furthermore, no between-Leader differences were found on the two dependent variables (voice quantity or quality) or the independent variable WMC. Table 1 shows an overview of how Leaders were perceived by participants on a 1 to 7 Likert scale.

16 Study 2 Method Before explaining the details of this experiment, we ask you to envision a typical meeting room, with about 10 people in it. One of those people is your team leader, who is sitting at the head of the table. The leader is talking about how to change the organization, and you have some ideas of your own you would like to suggest. Other people are voicing their ideas as well, drawing your attention away from how to formulate your own ideas. Some of the ideas of others are actually good, and you see your leader’s appreciation for these ideas. Other ideas are quite repetitive and do not seem to improve the discussion. While you listen to the ideas of others, you try to focus on which idea will still add novel and useful information to the discussion. What mentally happens while people try to make this decision, and how distraction of attention (thus WMC load) might affect such decisions, is what this second experiment is about. In the design of this experiment, we aimed to create a situation which matches the challenges described in the scenario above as closely as possible. The main purpose of this experiment, was to investigate what mentally happens while people select ideas to voice in a social context. Specifically, we aimed to explore whether loading WMC with another task (thus distracting attention away from voice), would affect the number of voiced ideas (quantity), and the selection of original and useful ideas (voice quality). Furthermore, we wanted to study whether the possible effect of WMC (load) on quantity or quality of voice would also appear within individuals, as opposed to only between individuals (Study 1). We thus designed two within- person conditions in this experiment, one with, and one without load on working memory. Participants were presented with the opportunity to voice ideas, while executing another task at the same time. This other task was either extremely easy (no WMC load) or quite difficult (high WMC load). Voice quantity was reflected in the number of ideas participants voiced in each condition. steps.title: Develop Dean Candidate Profiles
steps.instruction: Construct three fictional Dean candidate profiles (A, B, and C) based on student and expert evaluations to create an information-sharing task.

substeps.instruction: Interview 10 students to extract 20 important subjects for a new dean.
Conduct a 45-minute interview with a faculty Dean to evaluate the 20 statements on relative importance and practical feasibility.
Administer a 67-statement questionnaire to 283 students via Qualtrics, using a 5-point scale (1=negative, 5=positive) with emoticons.
Calculate the mean (M = 3.41, SD = 0.98) of all statements to establish a neutral reference point.
Categorize statements as negative (< 2.43), positive (> 4.39), or neutral (closest to the mean).
Compose profiles A (Scientific focus), B (Educational focus), and C (Science and Education balance) using a mix of positive, neutral, and negative statements.
Distribute statements as shared or unshared between the Leader and Follower roles according to the distribution in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

steps.title: Measure Visual Working Memory Capacity (WMC)
steps.instruction: Assess each participant's visual WMC using a delayed serial recognition task on a laptop.

substeps.instruction: Provide an on-screen explanation followed by four practice trials.
Administer 96 trials: present eight pictures sequentially in the center of the screen, each for 250 ms (total trial duration 2000 ms).
Implement a 1000 ms blank screen maintenance interval after the eight stimuli.
Present a single target picture and ask the participant to identify if it was 'old' (appeared in the series) or 'new'.
Ensure 50% of trials are no-change (old target) and 50% are change-trials (new target drawn from 130 items).
Calculate WMC using the formula: WMC = (% correct responses - 0.5) * (8 * 0.5), resulting in a capacity estimate between 0 and 8.

steps.title: Conduct Idea Generation Phase
steps.instruction: Collect a pool of personal ideas from participants to be used in the subsequent voice phase.

substeps.instruction: Ask participants to anonymously generate 10 problems, opinions, or suggestions for faculty improvement within 10 minutes.
Digitally classify each idea as 'low quality' or 'high quality' immediately upon entry.
Use these classifications to ensure an equal distribution of high and low quality ideas across the WMC load conditions.

steps.title: Perform WMC Load and Voice Practice
steps.instruction: Familiarize participants with the dual-task requirement of counting backwards while selecting information.

substeps.instruction: Practice the WMC load task: count backwards from 100 in steps of 2.
Practice a simple selection task: select the 3 largest animals from a list of 10 words while counting backwards.
Practice a complex selection task: select the 5 true statements about animals from a list of 10 sentences while counting backwards.

steps.title: Execute Communication and Load Manipulation Phase
steps.instruction: Measure voice quantity and quality while participants are under varying levels of cognitive load.

substeps.instruction: Present a 'window for voice' containing 10 messages: 5 of the participant's own ideas and 5 ideas from a database (representing a full quality range of 1-6).
Assign participants to two trials in random order of High vs. Low Load:
Low Load: Count backwards from 100 in steps of 0 (repeating the same number vocally).
High Load: Count backwards from 80 in steps of 2.
Allow participants to digitally select and send 'worthy' ideas to the experiment-leader.
Implement a financial incentive: €2.50 for correct counting, €1 bonus for voicing a high-quality idea, and €1 loss for voicing a low-quality idea.

steps.title: Evaluate Voice Quality
steps.instruction: Quantify and qualify the voice behavior exhibited during the experiment.

substeps.instruction: Measure voice quantity by counting the total number of ideas sent to the experimenter per load condition.
Have three independent judges rate the voiced ideas on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 6 (highly) based on whether they provided novel solutions or useful implementations superior to the status quo.
